extracted.intended_audience: students/scholars of humor, literary critics, and psychologists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and comparing theoretical criteria about what causes humor and what counts as 'humorous' from a scholarly treatment (historical and psychological) of laughter, tickling, benign humor, and mechanical/contrast theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tickling laughter depends on comical feeling (not mere touch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling laughter is 'probably not the effect of the common sensation but of feelings arising from the comicality of the situation.' Laughter in tickling can occur without tactile sensation (after anticipating it) and may accompany painful sensations if experienced in a playful context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanations that reduce tickling-laughter to simple tactile reflex; emphasize the subject's mood/play-attitude and perception of the situation as comical. Anti-pattern: treating ticklish laughter as purely sensory or as evidence of an intellectual 'conceptual factor' without acknowledging play/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play-attitude as necessary condition for ticklish/comic response
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'play-attitude' or particular mood that welcomes fun is a definite condition of the nervous system; when absent (alarm, illness, preoccupation, grief) tickling or playful overtures fail to produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the subject is in a pleasurable/playful state before attributing laughter to stimulus; examples from Sully and Darwin: children restrained by fear or illness do not respond with ticklish laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disappointment Theory (strained expectation causes laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter may arise from a 'strained expectation which comes to absolutely nothing' — a qualitative disappointment of an anticipated outcome leads to a humorous recoil (Aristotle/Kant/Hazlitt framing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiments (Dumont, Lillien J. Martin) and literary sources to assess whether humor hinges on thwarted expectations. Example: practical jokes rely on a prepared expectation that is subverted; anti-pattern: ignoring expectation/anticipation structure in a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness and contrast are core elements of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical reports and experiments indicate that an element of 'unexpectedness' and of 'contrast' is always present in things that provoke laughter; novelty or distortion relative to customary expectations often triggers mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging comic effect, look for a contrast (size, meaning, situation) and an unexpected displacement. Cross-cultural corroboration (Sanskrit treatises) supports primacy of novelty/distortion. Example: new things elicit laughter in children and 'savages' per commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity reduces comic quality (jokes wane with repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes lose value as they become familiar and easily anticipated; Hollingsworth measured rates at which various jokes 'wane' and found most jokes become vapid with repetition, though rates vary across joke types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score durability of a joke by its susceptibility to anticipation; expect poetic/meaningful jokes to endure longer than purely practical/absurd ones. Exception: a few jokes may increase in value on second/third acquaintance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic/meaningful jokes endure longer than practical/absurd ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes whose value lies in what they mean (poetic, semantic depth) tend to last longer in appreciation than jokes whose main value is the absurdity of not meaning what they seem to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lasting comic effects by investing in semantic or poetic content rather than only surprise/absurdity. Empirical basis: Hollingsworth's differential waning; anti-pattern: designing jokes relying solely on once-only practical surprisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign humor: absence of scorn, presence of affection/emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern notion of 'humor' emphasizes a genial, non-scornful quality — 'absence of scorn in humor, a presence of emotion' — true humor springs 'not more from the head than from the heart; ... its essence is love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish benign humor from satire/wit by looking for warmth, sympathy, and lack of contempt (Carlyle, Jean Paul, Hegel). Evaluate whether the comic fosters sympathy rather than derision; anti-pattern: conflating all laughter with scoffing or contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest humor invites sympathetic identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The most elevated form of comedy/humor invites the spectator's sympathy and involves characters who can rise above contradiction without bitterness — humor promotes compassion for human folly rather than derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comedic work for tendency to elicit identification with characters (Sahitya Darpana) and for treatment that 'elevates' rather than humiliates. Examples: Falstaff, Aristophanes cited by Hegel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/energy-overflow theory of laughter (Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is an overflow of nervous energy: when the mind is prepared for something big and receives something small instead, surplus energy discharges via laughter (muscles of voice, respiration, facial grimace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physiological/metaphorical energy-account to explain sudden laughter (acrobat/clown example). Limitations: does not fully account for all comic cases (e.g., aunt-in-closet example) and relies on vague notions like 'psychic weight.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Descending incongruity / contrast of great to small (Lipps/Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic often involves a 'descending incongruity' — attention moves from great things to small; the comic's second element is relatively meaningless or 'a relative nothing' that triggers a feeling of smallness (merriment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify pairs where the second term is 'for us relatively meaningless' (tiny house near palace, tiny baby among large ones) and treat the perceived descent as the comic pivot. Note Lipps' emphasis that smallness must be relative to our appetites/expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic feeling is sui generis (a unique feeling with 'merriment')
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipps argues 'the feeling of the comic is a feeling of the comic and nothing else' — it may be sometimes pleasurable and sometimes painful, but its ground-color is a kind of merriment (Heiterkeit), a feeling of lightness/smallness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying emotional responses, treat comic feeling as distinct from pure pleasure, pain, or contempt; look for an undercurrent of gaiety even in bittersweet laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic preparation vs stimulus demand governs seriousness vs gaiety
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation between the psychic energy a person has prepared and the demand of the object determines whether one experiences gravity (if demand > supply) or gaiety/merriment (if supply > demand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this metric to predict reactions: expecting something great but getting little yields celebratory laughter; expecting little but encountering great may produce seriousness or astonishment. Use examples (acrobat expecting somersault, clown dusting) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful annoyance (qualitative) vs mere quantitative disappointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic reaction more naturally arises from playful annoyances in a play-attitude than from simple quantitative disappointments; quantitatively small mismatches must be extreme enough to prevent serious adjustment to become comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between trivial quantitative gaps (which may not provoke laughter) and those so extreme or prolonged that they become ludicrous. Example: clown meticulously dusting a horse's flank becomes comic because it defeats adjustment and persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition effects vary by joke type (not uniform vapidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Though repetition tends to make jokes vapid, different types of jokes wane at different rates; some initially top-rated jokes become poorest later, while others may even gain on subsequent exposures (Hollingsworth curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a joke's longevity empirically across repeated exposures; design for forms (poetic/meaningful) that resist rapid waning. Anti-pattern: assuming all comic effects behave identically under repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-linguistic criterion: 'humor' denotes genial, empathetic comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'humor' historically shifted from physiological temperaments to denote genial, eccentric, or affectionate comic tendencies; modern usage tends to privilege genial excursions of comic spirit over satirical bitterness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing or producing humor, prefer treatments that align with the modern 'humor' sense (sympathy, genial eccentricity) when seeking 'the sense of humor' as described in modern literature; be conscious of cultural/historical connotations when invoking the term.
